summary: On Capy, the 'own lease' check is true for every install after any gstack skill has started on the machine, so the self-upgrade turns off for the rest of the machine's life instead of only for the /ship run. bin/gstack-skill-start writes its lease for gstack_harness_pid, which skips past shells to the first ancestor that is not a shell. On a Capy machine every bash call is a direct child of the one long-lived capy-server process, which all threads and subagents on that machine share, so the lease names capy-server's pid. That lease stays alive as long as capy-server runs (its start identity still matches), and every later install.sh run has capy-server in its ancestry. The result: `live` succeeds, `live --exclude-ancestry-of $$` finds nothing, and the new branch prints 'this session's own gstack run holds a workflow lease … deferred until the run ends' every time. That includes a new session on the same machine and runs long after /ship has finished. The CHANGELOG says 'a run with no live lease of its own upgrades as before', but that never happens on Capy, and the trailer stays ok with behind=, so lanes keep running the stale revision without anything failing. The new test misses this because it leases a short-lived `bash -c` pid that exits before the second install.
fix: Key the deferral on the run itself, not on the harness ancestor. For example, have workflows that run an install from inside themselves (/ship's docs step) export a marker that the install checks, or lease a per-run pid with --pid/--from. Alternatively, ignore an own-ancestry lease whose pid is the machine-wide harness (the nearest non-shell ancestor of the install itself). Add a test where the lease holder is a long-lived ancestor shared by two separate install runs.
evidence: bin/gstack-skill-start:66,129 (PARENT_PID=$(gstack_harness_pid "$PPID"); gstack-lease touch --pid "$PARENT_PID"); bin/gstack-harness-pid.sh walks up to the first ancestor that is not a shell; bin/gstack-lease state() keeps a lease alive as long as the pid's identity matches, at any age; on this Capy machine `ps` shows every tool-call bash with ppid 361, which is capy-server.

label: FIXABLE
summary: On Capy machines, the "own lease" check turns off the session-start self-upgrade for every thread on the machine, indefinitely. Location: bin/gstack-capy-session:114-116. How it happens: bin/gstack-skill-start writes the lease under gstack_harness_pid, which climbs past shell processes to the first non-shell ancestor. On a Capy machine that ancestor is capy-server, one long-lived process (pid 361 here, parent of every tool bash call) shared by all threads and subagents. As a result, every skill start on the machine writes the same lease file, `<git dir>/gstack-leases/361`, and capy-server is also in the ancestry of every later install. The new condition is "some live lease exists AND none is outside my ancestry". After any gstack skill has started on the machine, that condition is true for every install-mode run on the machine, including a fresh thread's session start that runs no workflow at all. Why it never clears: the lease has no release verb. state() reports a lease with a matching identity as alive for as long as capy-server runs. The 120-minute prune only runs during a later `touch`, and each skill start re-touches the same file and refreshes its mtime anyway. So "deferred until the run ends" really means "deferred until capy-server restarts". Reproduced, without touching the checkout, using GSTACK_LEASE_DIR pointed at a scratch directory under <home>/.capy/work: - In one bash call: `gstack-lease touch --pid $(gstack_harness_pid $$)` wrote the file `361`. - In a separate, unrelated bash call: `gstack-lease live` printed `361 0m capy-server` and exited 0, and `gstack-lease live --exclude-ancestry-of $$` exited 1. Both halves of the line 114-116 condition are therefore true, and the upgrade branch is skipped with UPGRADE_BUSY. Effect in production: Capy installs stop following origin/main. They stay between the floor and the tip, with a permanent `WARN behind`. This is the opposite of the file's own contract ("Always current when online"). The trailer stays ok, so nothing fails loudly and the drift goes unnoticed. The new test misses this because it uses a short-lived holder shell that exits, and that is not the production topology. Fix: decide "this session's own run" from a signal scoped to the current workflow, not from ancestry. Options: an explicit environment marker exported by the workflow (for example, /ship exporting a run marker that install.sh checks), or a lease keyed on something narrower than the harness pid. At minimum, treat a holder that is a known shared host process (capy-server) as not proving an in-flight run. Add a test where the lease holder is a long-lived ancestor shared with an unrelated install.

summary: The CHANGELOG, docs/troubleshooting.md and the REASON string all make a false claim. Locations: bin/gstack-capy-session:121, docs/troubleshooting.md upgrade-busy section, CHANGELOG [Unreleased]. All three say the upgrade is "deferred until the run ends". summary: A race between the two `live` scans can name another session's lease as "this session's own" and skip an upgrade that should have run. Location: bin/gstack-capy-session:115-116. OWN comes from the first scan, which is unfiltered. The "no foreign lease" verdict comes from a second, separate scan. If a foreign holder dies, or its lease is reclaimed as stale, between the two scans, the second scan comes back empty. The skip message then lists the foreign pid as the caller's own run, and the self-upgrade is skipped even though no live holder remains. Each scan can also reclaim stale leases on its own, so the two scans can see different sets of files. Fix: do one `live` scan and split its rows by membership in the `--exclude-ancestry-of` set, for example by running `live --exclude-ancestry-of` once and taking the difference from a single snapshot, or by adding an `--only-ancestry-of` mode to gstack-lease.

summary: The new branch runs before gstack-upgrade's other refusals, so the code it reports can be wrong. Location: bin/gstack-capy-session:114. Dirty, diverged, pinned and Bun-hold refusals are never reached when an own lease exists. label: INVESTIGATE
summary: This is a pre-existing gap that the change builds on. On Capy, the harness-pid lease cannot tell sibling agents apart: they all share capy-server's pid. bin/gstack-upgrade's "own chain never counts" rule therefore already treated every sibling's lease as the caller's own, so before this change leases never blocked an upgrade on a shared Capy machine. The change flips that from "never blocks" to "always blocks" (finding 1) without fixing the underlying identity problem. That identity needs a human design decision: a per-thread or per-workflow lease key instead of the harness pid.

label: Medium
summary: A finishing sibling workflow bypasses the caller's own lease protection `bin/gstack-capy-session:114–116` skips the upgrade only when live leases exist AND none belongs to another process chain. If the caller and a sibling both hold leases, the second probe succeeds, so the wrapper falls through to `gstack-upgrade` at line 127. If the sibling finishes before the upgrader checks leases, the upgrader excludes the caller's ancestry and sees no remaining blocker. It then fast-forwards the installation underneath the still-running caller—the exact mid-/ship revision change this patch is meant to prevent. The upgrader performs remote discovery and fetching before its lease check, so the sibling can finish during ordinary network waits; this is not limited to a tiny instruction-level window. Defer the install-mode self-upgrade whenever the initial probe finds any live lease (unless explicitly forced), or positively detect an ancestral holder without making that protection conditional on the absence of foreign holders. Add a regression with both holders present at the wrapper probe and the foreign holder exiting before the upgrader probe. The added test covers only the sole-holder case.

The new own-lease deferral branch has a documented override (GSTACK_UPGRADE_FORCE=1 still upgrades; CHANGELOG and docs/troubleshooting.md promise it) but the new test covers only the deferred path and the no-lease path. Nothing fails if the FORCE guard on line 114 is dropped or inverted, which would leave an install inside /ship with no way to upgrade.
fix: Add a row to the #3571 test: under the same lease-holding shell, run the install with GSTACK_UPGRADE_FORCE=1 and assert `SELF_UPGRADE: done 1.0.1 -> 1.0.2` and HEAD == f.c.

summary: On Capy, the own-lease check matches a lease that never ends, so after any gstack workflow has run on a machine, the install-mode self-upgrade is deferred for as long as that machine runs. bin/gstack-skill-start leases gstack_harness_pid, which is the first non-shell ancestor. On a Capy machine that ancestor is the machine-wide capy-server process (measured here: harness=364 capy-server, running about 5.8 h, the parent of every bash call from every thread and subagent). Nothing ever releases a lease: gstack-lease has only touch, live and list. `live` ignores age when a lease carries a start identity. The only prune, `-mmin +120`, runs inside `touch`, which rewrites the same pid first. So line 115 succeeds and line 116 finds nothing outside the caller's ancestry on every later install, whether or not a /ship is running. The run never ends, so 'deferred until the run ends' never happens. The self-upgrade (the 'always current when online' contract) is off until the next machine restart, with only a WARN and behind=. The message also calls other threads' runs on a shared machine 'this session's own run'. The new test does not model this: its holder is a short-lived bash shell, so the 'after the run' upgrade passes only because that shell exits.
fix: Tie the deferral to a signal that ends with the run, not to the harness-pid lease. One option: /ship's docs step (or gstack-skill-start, as an exported run marker) runs the install with GSTACK_CAPY_SELF_UPGRADE=off, or with a GSTACK_RUN_ID that the session script checks. Another: require a recent lease mtime. Add a test where the lease holder is a long-lived non-shell ancestor that outlives the workflow, and assert that a later install with no workflow running still upgrades.

summary: 1. [HIGH, FIXABLE] On a Capy machine, "this session's own run holds a lease" is true for every install after any gstack skill has ever started there, so self-upgrade is effectively disabled for good. (bin/gstack-capy-session, the new elif at about lines 114-124) How it happens: bin/gstack-skill-start writes the lease as `gstack-lease touch --pid "$PARENT_PID"`, where PARENT_PID is gstack_harness_pid, the first ancestor that is not a shell. On a Capy machine that ancestor is the machine-wide capy-server. On this machine it resolves to `364 1 capy-server`, the parent of every bash call from every thread and shared subagent. So every lease on the machine is named 364, and every install's ancestry, $$ -> bash -> 364, contains it. Three facts in gstack-lease keep that lease alive: there is no release verb, nothing deletes a lease when its workflow ends, and `state()` ignores age whenever the record holds a valid identity. The 120-minute prune runs only inside `touch`, and each new skill start rewrites the same file 364, so that file is never pruned. Reproduced in a scratch GSTACK_LEASE_DIR (/tmp, nothing written to the checkout): I wrote a lease from a plain bash call with no workflow running and backdated it 3 days. `gstack-lease list` then printed `364 4320m alive`, `live` printed `364 4320m capy-server` (rc=0), and `live --exclude-ancestry-of $$` returned rc=1. That is exactly the pair of results the new condition treats as "own lease, defer". Production effect: the header promises "always current when online", but every install-mode session start after the first skill run on the machine prints `SELF_UPGRADE: skipped (this session's own gstack run holds a workflow lease … (UPGRADE_BUSY))` until capy-server restarts or its identity changes. The trailer stays `ok … behind=N`, so lanes keep running on a stale gstack with only a note. Above the floor nothing moves the checkout any more. The message also blames "this session's own run" when the real holder is often an unrelated, finished workflow from another thread on the same machine. The test's second half ("after that shell exits it upgrades") cannot happen in production, because the holder is capy-server and it does not exit. Fix: stop inferring "own run" from process ancestry, which is useless when the harness pid is a machine-wide daemon. Options: (a) have the workflow export a run-scoped marker, such as a lease token or GSTACK_WORKFLOW_LEASE=<id>, that the install's environment inherits, and defer only when that marker names a live lease; (b) add a release on workflow end plus an age cap in `live` for identity-bearing leases; (c) at minimum, ignore own-chain leases whose mtime is older than the prune window. Add a test where the lease holder is a long-lived non-shell ancestor that never exits.

summary: 2. [MEDIUM, INVESTIGATE] The same ancestry collapse means the fix gives no per-run protection on Capy, and the recommended manual fix bypasses the lease for concurrent runs. (bin/gstack-capy-session new branch and its printed `fix: $ROOT/bin/gstack-upgrade`; docs/troubleshooting.md) Every Capy session on a machine shares ancestor 364, and bin/gstack-upgrade excludes the caller's ancestry. So the printed fix, run from any thread on that machine, excludes the only lease there is and fast-forwards the checkout under whichever /ship is mid-run in another thread or shared subagent. That is the #3571 failure mode, with the new message actively steering people into it. The docs now say the Capy install "counts" the caller's own session, which suggests per-run isolation that the pid model cannot provide. Process ancestry is part of the lease design itself, so whether the lease should key on something other than the harness pid on Capy needs a human decision.

summary: 4. [LOW, FIXABLE] The two `gstack-lease live` calls race (TOCTOU), and the first one gains a new side effect. (the new elif) Own-ness is computed as "the first call without exclusion finds a lease AND the second call with exclusion finds none". Fix: make one `live` call that reports which leases are inside the ancestry versus outside it (or add a `--only-ancestry-of` mode) and decide from that single snapshot.

summary: Medium — A second lease can bypass the caller's own upgrade protection (`bin/gstack-capy-session:114–127`). The new guard skips upgrading only when there are live leases AND no leases outside the caller's ancestry. If both the current workflow and another workflow hold leases, the second query succeeds, so execution falls through to `gstack-upgrade`. That command performs network discovery and fetching before checking leases, and its check deliberately excludes the caller's ancestry (`bin/gstack-upgrade:78–99,209–220`). If the other workflow finishes during that interval, the upgrader sees no blocking lease and fast-forwards the installation while the caller's workflow still holds its lease. This recreates the mid-/ship version change this patch is intended to prevent, allowing receipt rules and helper implementations to change partway through the run. It requires neither the force override nor a malformed lease. Skip the automatic upgrade whenever the initial query finds any live lease, or explicitly detect an own-ancestry holder independently of whether foreign holders exist. Add a regression with both an own and a foreign lease, releasing the foreign holder after the session's queries but before the upgrader's lease check; HEAD must remain unchanged.
